latin.156:
§. XIII.
Ope Distinctionis, superiori §.XII traditae, in facili est decidere, & vel justè, vel nefariè, decisam deprehendere Quaestionum Theologico-Historicarum bigam: Utrum Reformati Augustanae Confessionis Socii? &, Utrum Pacis Religiosae participes iidem habendi?
latin.157: Utriusque, cumprimis posterioris, affirmativam veram & prioris Veritatem necessariò supponentem inferentemque, prolixius evicerunt Joh. Crocius, Tractatu Germanico suprâ allegato, & Commentario suo spissiori, quaestione secunda, Auctor item der ausführlichen Behauptung à pag. 90. ad 111., Georgius Pauli in Reformato Augustano, & Venerandus Facultatis nostrae Senior contra Liebhardum cap. 4. & sexto integris, inter alias probationes, maximè ex Comitio Anni 1566. Augustano (de quo prolixissimè Joh. Crocius cit. Comment. Cap. 18.) Cap. 4. §. 8. pag. 102.;
latin.158: Praetereà Cap. 6. §. 8., Articuli VII. Instrumenti Pacis ut notatu dignissima ita celebratissima verba adducens, quibus Reformati disertè Augustanae Confessionis Sociis annumerantur, omniaque inimica & Achristianô exemplo, Sanguinem Christianum sitientia temerè tumultuantium nonnullorum Theologorum acerborum molimina, ictu unô prosternuntur. Verba Instrumenti Pacifici ita habent: Unanimi quoque Caesareae Majestatis omniumque Imperii Ordinum Consensu placuit, ut quicquid Juris aut beneficii, cum omnes aliae Constitutiones Imperii, tùm Pax Religionis & Publica haec Transactio in eaque decisio gravaminum, caeteris Catholicis & Augustanae Confessionis addictis Statibus & Subditis tribuunt, id etiam iis, qui inter eos Reformati vocantur, competere debeat.
latin.159: Verba haec, contra verè pedanticos Criticos, egregiè vindicavit nuperrimus Auctor der gründliche Vorstellung/ welche das einige wahre Mittel zur Vereinigung der beyden Evangelischen Religionen in Deutschland sey/ pag. 11. 9.8. nobis alibi, in ingenua scilicet in Arminianismus Inquisitione nostra, pag. 302. citatus laudatusque.
latin.160: Neque hîc sibi ipsis infesti sunt Reformati, quando cum Neostadianis Theologis Cap. IV. à pag. 143. de Augustana Confessione, contra hos, qui eam, tantum non Sacrae Scripturae aequiparatum eunt, annotant (id quod Calovius, iniquè profectò & non nisi per convitium, Calviniana convitia interpretatur, Crit. Sacr. pag. 68.) Esse eam scriptam annis non ita multis post Reformationis initium, in quo non tam subitò potuerunt omnia perspici & explicari &c. &c.
latin.161: Nam aliud est, August. Confess. convitiis proscindere, vel quoquô modô debitam illius Auctoritatem elevare (quod à Reformatorum nemine unquam designatum est) aliud, non permittere velle, quòd humanum Scriptum, eóque errori obnoxium, cum infallibili Dei verbo, in eundem censum veniat. Rem omnem ex professo excutit Crocius Comment. cap. 36. a p. 497. Calvini Judicium de Augustana Confessione, ab eo promptè aliàs subscribenda, imò actu ipso subscripta (uti testatur in Epistola sua ad Martinum Schalingium Pastorem Ratisbonensem Anno 1557., Epistolarum Tomô, non ita pridem cum Operibus omnibus Amstelodami editô, p. m. 112.), quando Aug. Confessionem facem furiae Gallicae alicubi appellitat, genuino suo sensui restitutum lege, tùm apud Pareum Fren. p. 294, tùm apud Auctorem der ausführlichen Behauptung p. 74. & seqq. omniumq; plenissimè apud Joh. Crocium, Comment. saepius citat. p. 514. 515. 518.

pass_a.156: §. XIII. By the aid of the Distinction handed down in the preceding §.XII, it is easy to decide, and to detect as decided either justly or nefariously, the pair of Theological-Historical Questions: Whether the Reformed are Associates of the Augsburg Confession? and, Whether the same are to be held participants of the Religious Peace?
pass_a.157: The true affirmative of each — especially of the latter, which necessarily presupposes and infers the truth of the former — Joh. Crocius has more fully proved in the German Tract alleged above and in his thicker Commentary, question the second; likewise the Author of the ausführlichen Behauptung from p. 90 to 111; Georgius Pauli in the Reformato Augustano; and the Venerable Senior of our Faculty against Liebhard in chapters 4 and 6 entire, among other proofs, chiefly from the Augsburg Diet of the Year 1566 (of which Joh. Crocius cites most fully in Comment. Cap. 18), Cap. 4 §. 8 p. 102;
pass_a.158: Besides Cap. 6 §. 8., bringing forward the words of Article VII of the Instrument of Peace — as most worthy of note, so most celebrated — by which the Reformed are expressly numbered among the Associates of the Augsburg Confession, and all the hostile and, by an un-Christian example, Christian-blood-thirsting endeavors of certain harsher theologians rashly tumultuating are laid low with one blow. The words of the Pacific Instrument run thus: It has likewise pleased by the unanimous Consent of the Imperial Majesty and of all the Estates of the Empire, that whatever of Right or benefit the other Constitutions of the Empire, as also the Peace of Religion and this Public Transaction and the decision of grievances therein, assign to the other States and Subjects addicted to the Catholic and to the Augsburg Confession, that same ought also to belong to those who among them are called Reformed.
pass_a.159: These words, against truly pedantic Critics, the most recent Author of der gründliche Vorstellung / welche das einige wahre Mittel zur Vereinigung der beyden Evangelischen Religionen in Deutschland sey / has excellently vindicated at pag. 11. 9.8. — cited and praised by us elsewhere, namely in our Ingenua in Arminianismus Inquisitio, pag. 302.
pass_a.160: Nor are the Reformed here hostile to themselves, when with the Neostadian Theologians in Cap. IV from p. 143 concerning the Augsburg Confession they note against those who go nearly to equate it with Sacred Scripture (which Calovius, unfairly indeed and not except by insult, interprets as Calvinian insults, Crit. Sacr. p. 68.) That it was written not so many years after the beginning of the Reformation, in which not so suddenly could all things be seen through and explained, &c. &c.
pass_a.161: For it is one thing to tear the Augsburg Confession with insults, or in any way to lessen its due Authority (which was never marked out by any of the Reformers), another to be unwilling to permit that a human Writing, and therefore liable to error, should come into the same census with the infallible word of God. Crocius examines the whole matter professedly in Comment. cap. 36 from p. 497. Calvin's Judgment concerning the Augsburg Confession — to be subscribed by him promptly at other times, nay subscribed in the very act (as he testifies in his Letter to Martin Schalingius, Pastor of Regensburg, in the Year 1557, in the Volume of Letters not so long ago edited at Amsterdam with all the Works, p. m. 112.) — when he somewhere calls the Augsburg Confession a torch of Gallic fury, read restored to its genuine sense, both in Pareus Fren. p. 294, and in the Author of the ausführlichen Behauptung p. 74 and following, and most fully of all in Joh. Crocius, Comment. often cited, pp. 514, 515, 518.

156: §. XIII. With the distinction given in §.XII above, it is easy to settle — and to see whether the settlement was just or wicked — this pair of theological-historical questions:
Are the Reformed associates of the Augsburg Confession? And are they to be counted participants in the Religious Peace?
157: On both questions — especially the second, which must presuppose and imply the first — the affirmative is true.

Joh. Crocius proved it at length in the German tract already cited and in his denser Commentary, question 2; so did the author of the Ausführliche Behauptung, pp. 90–111; Georgius Pauli in the Reformatus Augustanus; and the venerable Senior of our faculty against Liebhard in chapters 4 and 6 entire.
Among other proofs they lean chiefly on the Augsburg Diet of 1566 (treated most fully by Crocius, Comm. Cap. 18), Cap. 4 §.8 p. 102;
158: Further, Cap. 6 §.8 cites the famous words of Article VII of the Peace Instrument — worth noting, and celebrated — by which the Reformed are expressly counted among Augsburg Confession associates.
With that one stroke fall the hostile schemes of certain harsh theologians who, in an un-Christian way, rashly riot as if thirsting for Christian blood.

The Peace Instrument's words run: By unanimous consent of the Imperial Majesty and of all Estates of the Empire it was resolved that whatever right or benefit the other constitutions of the Empire, the Religious Peace, and this public settlement (with its decision of grievances) grant to other Catholic and Augsburg-Confession states and subjects, that same must also belong to those among them called Reformed.
159: Against truly pedantic critics, the newest author of the Gründliche Vorstellung (Which Is the One True Means for Uniting the Two Evangelical Religions in Germany) has finely defended these words at pp. 11 and 98.
We cited and praised that author elsewhere — namely in our Ingenua in Arminianismus Inquisitio, p. 302.
160: Nor are the Reformed here their own enemies when, with the Neustadt theologians (Cap. IV from p. 143) on the Augsburg Confession, they note against those who nearly equate it with Holy Scripture — which Calovius unfairly, and only by insult, reads as "Calvinian insults" (Crit. Sacr. p. 68).
They note that it was written not many years after the Reformation began, when not everything could suddenly be seen through and explained, and so on.
161: For it is one thing to tear the Augsburg Confession with insults, or somehow to lower its due authority — which no Reformer ever set out to do — and another to refuse to let a human writing, liable to error, stand in the same rank as God's infallible word.
Crocius works the whole question through in Comm. cap. 36 from p. 497.

As for Calvin's judgment on the Augsburg Confession: he was ready to subscribe it at other times, and in fact did subscribe it (see his 1557 letter to Martin Schalingius, pastor at Regensburg, in the Letters volume lately edited at Amsterdam with the Opera, p. 112).

When elsewhere he calls the Augsburg Confession a torch of Gallic fury, read that restored to its genuine sense — in Pareus (Fren. p. 294), in the Ausführliche Behauptung (p. 74ff.), and most fully in Crocius (Comm. pp. 514, 515, 518).
